name: Hunter eyes

lead: Hunter eyes describes an eye area that looks intense and masculine: deep-set, slightly hooded, with a positive canthal tilt, little visible white below the iris and low-set brows. It is contrasted with so-called prey eyes that are rounder, show more white and tilt downward.

Users attribute the look to bone structure such as orbit shape, brow ridge and cheekbone support, plus soft-tissue factors like lid hooding. The term has no formal definition in ophthalmology or anthropology, and no study has tested it as a category.

paras: People approximate the look with grooming and makeup, such as brow shaping, eyeliner and lash styling, and by lowering body fat to show the orbital area. Some try squinting or exercises, though users disagree on whether those change anything; surgical options discussed include canthoplasty, upper blepharoplasty and orbital procedures.

The concept itself carries no direct risk. Surgical and filler procedures talked about for the look carry standard risks such as asymmetry, dry eye, vision-related complications and revision surgery. Some critics link the trend to appearance anxiety.

angle.text: Hunter eyes are described online as an ideal eye area: a positive tilt, deep set and low brows that give an intense, masculine gaze. Users approximate it with grooming and makeup, and some try squinting or exercises. The term has no formal medical definition.

lead: Hunter eyes is a looksmaxxing term for an eye area that looks narrow, deep-set and intense. The features usually listed are a positive canthal tilt (the outer corner sits higher than the inner corner), little upper-eyelid exposure, low-set eyebrows and little visible white below the iris.[1][2] The contrasting label, 'prey eyes', describes rounder eyes with more visible white and a downward tilt.[2] People pursue the look because it is widely described in these communities as masculine and striking, and the routes they discuss range from makeup and lash styling to eyelid and orbital surgery.[2][3][4]

The term is slang rather than a clinical category. Grokipedia states that it has no formal definition in medical, anthropological or ophthalmological literature, and that no peer-reviewed research validates 'hunter' and 'prey' as human eye categories.[2] The individual components, however, are studied in plastic surgery and ophthalmology, particularly canthal tilt, palpebral fissure shape and brow-to-lid distance, and published work links several of them to ratings of attractiveness.[5][6][5]

According to Wikipedia, the phrase originated on incel message boards in the 2010s, stayed on obscure forums for some years, and was popularised on TikTok in the 2020s by mostly male creators.[1] On looksmax.org the topic has run for years, with threads praising it as a top-tier trait, calling it overrated, or arguing that eye shape is determined by bone and cannot be trained.[7][3][4][8][9][10][11][12]

paras: Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists hunter eyes among the facial features that community members assess when judging male attractiveness, defining them as a positive canthal tilt, little to no upper-eyelid exposure and low-set eyebrows, and noting the comparison with the eye area of a predatory animal.[1] Grokipedia adds deep-set placement, an almond-like shape, hooded upper lids, minimal scleral show beneath the iris and an intense gaze, and describes an 'almond hunter hybrid' variant discussed in the same circles.[2]

Anatomically, the article attributes the look to the position of the canthal tendons, the shape of the bony orbit, brow prominence and the height of the palpebral fissure.[2] Forum members add vocabulary such as orbital vector (how far the eyeball projects relative to the cheekbone and lower lid) and 'infras' (infraorbital support), and use it to separate the look from other attractive eye types. One looksmax.org thread argues that a good eye area does not automatically count as hunter eyes, and another describes 'high appeal' eyes that lack the hunter label because they are slightly larger or have more recessed lower-lid support.[3][4] Another thread argues the look is distinct from hooded eyes in general.[12]

Wikipedia describes the term as a neologism from incel message boards in the 2010s, rooted in manosphere discussion of the 'Chad' ideal and in forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, which collectively formed the 'PSL community' that created the PSL rating scale.[1] Grokipedia likewise dates the term to the mid-2010s and says it moved to Reddit and then TikTok.[2] Older looksmax.org threads carry titles from early years of the site, among them threads calling the look extremely intimidating, a meme, or giga rare, and a thread asking whether it can be achieved without surgery.[7][9][11][13]

On TikTok, Wikipedia notes, early looksmaxxing content was often framed as self-improvement with self-deprecating humour, while by the mid-2020s mainstream coverage more often linked the topic to blackpill ideology.[1] Coverage of looksmaxxing generally has appeared in outlets including the BBC, The Guardian, The New York Times, Business Insider, Vice and The Conversation, according to Wikipedia's list; these pieces discuss the movement as a whole rather than this single feature.[1]

sections.h: Features and how they are measured
paras: Canthal tilt is typically measured as the angle between a horizontal line and a line through the inner and outer corners of the eye. Plastic surgery and ophthalmology papers use the measure when describing eyelid and orbital procedures, congenital conditions and attractiveness.[5][6] Grokipedia cites twin and measurement studies when it says that periorbital traits are heritable and that eye-area measurements have been related to attractiveness.[2]

Forum users also discuss eyelid hooding, the amount of sclera visible, eyebrow height and fat or fluid under the eyes. In threads comparing eye types, users link low scleral show and recessed lower-lid support to the hunter look, and link rounder, more exposed eyes to the prey look.[2][4]

Non-surgical approaches mentioned in communities and in Grokipedia's summary include eyeliner and lash techniques that extend and lift the outer corner, brow shaping, managing puffiness through sleep, hydration and diet, and facial exercises or 'mewing'.[2] Wikipedia notes that people also rub the orbital area, practise mewing or seek surgery, and that researchers have argued the evidence does not support changes in facial structure from such methods.[1]

On looksmax.org one user asks how to correct an asymmetry from 'hunter eyes training' and receives replies that eye shape follows bone structure and that no exercise changes it; another reply says implants or surgery are needed to reach the look.[8] Surgery options named in the community and in Grokipedia include canthoplasty, upper blepharoplasty, orbital decompression or implants, and fillers.[2] A looksmax.org thread titled as a surgery result shows how users present outcomes of such procedures.[14]
No studies found on hunter eyes as a defined category. Related research examines its components, and these studies are described here for context only.

A 2007 experimental study in Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery by Bashour and Geist tested medial canthal tilt as a cue in female facial attractiveness; judges made forced choices between unmodified female faces and versions in which the tilt had been exaggerated in Photoshop, and the exaggerated version was chosen 93 percent of the time.[6][5] The authors suggested the cue may relate to neotenic and sexually dimorphic features of palpebral fissure inclination.[5]

A 2026 analysis in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery examined nine periocular measurements in 3,517 Asian adults from a public database against AI-derived attractiveness scores. Higher scores were associated with a smaller brow-to-lid distance, a smaller intercanthal distance, a larger outer canthal angle and greater canthal tilt, with brow-to-lid and intercanthal distance showing the strongest inverse associations.[5][6] A 2026 cross-sectional survey of 763 participants in Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery found that an upward lateral canthal tilt strongly influenced perceived femininity in digitally altered periocular images.[5]

Surgical research also reports on canthal tilt as an outcome. A 2026 anatomical and retrospective study of an orbital soft-tissue suspension technique for lateral hooding in 85 East Asian patients reported an increase in lateral canthal tilt of about 5 degrees; a 2026 uncontrolled cohort of 22 women who had barbed thread lifts reported increased lateral canthal tilt at 6 and 12 months; and a 2026 pilot of three patients receiving a polycaprolactone injectable reported increased canthal tilt.[5] In a single-surgeon series of 78 lower-blepharoplasty patients, negative preoperative canthal tilt was linked to scleral show, and the authors reported high satisfaction.[5] Most of these studies were retrospective or uncontrolled, and none addressed the hunter-eyes label.[5] A 2023 study used AI to measure 100 facial points in 42 Caucasian celebrities to quantify sexual dimorphism in aesthetic faces.[6]

Wikipedia lists coverage of looksmaxxing in the BBC (2024, 2026), The Guardian (2024), Business Insider (2023), The New York Times (2023), Vice (2023), The Conversation (2024), NPR (2026), Vanity Fair (2026) and The New Yorker (2026), and cites academic work by Halpin and colleagues (2025) and Sousbois (2025) on masculinity and surgical body design.[1] A 2026 editorial in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open by Maini and Janis addresses ethical implications of looksmaxxing and male beauty standards for plastic surgeons.[5]

Grokipedia reports critics who link the hunter-eyes trend to body-dysmorphia concerns among young men, to Eurocentric beauty standards and to the commercial growth of eye-makeup trends such as 'fox eyes'.[2] Community members themselves are divided: a looksmax.org thread argues that hunter eyes look uncanny and that good eyes do not require them, while others describe them as a core appeal trait.[3][4]

Threads argue both that hunter eyes are highly desirable and that they are overrated or look unusual, and some argue that 'too much forward growth' or the hunter label is a meme.[3][4][10][11] The term sits in a vocabulary alongside canthal tilt, orbital vector, hooded eyes and 'high appeal' eyes, and the concept is used in photo-rating threads where members assess one another's eye areas.[4][9]

The concept itself carries no direct risk. Eyelid, canthal and orbital procedures carry the usual risks of surgery, including asymmetry, dry eye, scarring, changes in lid position and the possibility of revision, and some users in forum threads report distress about perceived eye-shape flaws.[2][8]

lore.intro: Hunter eyes is a staple of looksmax.org eye-area discussion, with sharply divided opinions about whether it is the top eye trait, a meme, or something only bone structure or surgery can deliver.[3][4][8][11]

timeline.event: Bashour and Geist publish an experiment showing exaggerated medial canthal tilt is strongly preferred in female faces.[5]
The term 'hunter eyes' emerges on incel and looksmaxxing forums, according to Wikipedia and Grokipedia.[1][2]
A looksmax.org thread simply titled 'Hunter eyes' is among the site's longer-running discussions of the feature.[7]
TikTok creators popularise the term and looksmaxxing vocabulary to a mass audience.[1]
Business Insider, The New York Times and Vice publish pieces on looksmaxxing, per Wikipedia's coverage list.[1]
Looksmax.org threads debate whether hunter eyes matter, are overrated, or 'are appeal'.[3][4]
Studies on periocular measurements and AI attractiveness scores in Asian adults, and an editorial on looksmaxxing ethics in plastic surgery, are published.[5][6]
